The underrepresentation of women and racial and ethnic minorities in clinical trials has been documented across decades of pharmaceutical research, and three studies are particularly relevant to the questions examined here.

@Poon2013 examined the participation of women and the reporting of sex-stratified analyses in 156 late-phase pivotal trials supporting FDA approval from 2000 to 2009. Women constituted, on average, 45% of enrolled participants, with the greatest imbalances in cardiovascular and infectious disease trials. Crucially, even when women were enrolled in adequate numbers, sex-specific analyses were rarely reported. Fewer than one-third of trials provided subgroup results stratified by sex. This finding maps directly onto the ACTG 320 sex subgroup problem: female participants dominated enrollment (82.6%) while the male stratum contributed only 15 events, leaving the sex-specific comparison severely underpowered regardless of total enrollment.

@Khan2020 extended the question to racial and ethnic minorities, analyzing pivotal cardiometabolic drug trials submitted to the FDA between 2008 and 2017. Minority enrollment improved only modestly over the decade and remained well below the representation of those groups among patients with the diseases under study. The authors noted the same structural problem visible in ACTG 320: even when minority participants were enrolled, absolute numbers were too small to support meaningful subgroup analyses. They conclude by calling for prospective enrollment targets for underrepresented groups as a design requirement rather than a post-hoc 
consideration.

@Eshera2015 documented the same pattern across all therapeutic areas in pivotal trials from 2005 to 2012, finding persistent underrepresentation of older adults, women, and racial minorities relative to disease burden in the general population. Taken together, these three studies establish that the limitations visible in ACTG 320 are not unique to HIV research but reflect a structural feature of how pivotal trials are designed. The absence of significant subgroup findings in these trials typically reflects insufficient power rather than an absence of heterogeneous treatment effects. A distinction that this paper quantifies explicitly using the ACTG 320 data.
